subject: english-literature
title: Meter and Music
welcome_lead: Beneath every poem beats a metrical heart. Scan iambs, anapaests and trochees — the music behind the meaning.
meta_desc: Iambic pentameter, anapaestic and trochaic meter at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You have learned to scan — and to hear the meaning a poet smuggles in beneath the stress.

concepts.def: Five iambs per line (de-DUM x5); the dominant meter of Shakespeare and much English verse.
Two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed (di-di-DUM); galloping, often comic or martial.
Stressed-unstressed (DUM-de); falling, urgent (Blake's 'Tyger Tyger burning bright').
Two stressed syllables together (heart-break); often disrupts a regular meter for emphasis.
The marking of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line to reveal its meter.
Replacing an expected foot with another (a trochaic foot in iambic line) to disrupt rhythm meaningfully.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Iambic pentameter mirrors English speech rhythms. Shakespeare's Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? falls into five iambs.

Departures from the pattern (trochaic substitution at the line start) carry interpretive weight.

Browning's I sprang to the stirrup, and Joris, and he uses anapaests to evoke a horse's gallop.

Anapaestic rhythm is light, propulsive — common in comic verse and military songs.

Trochaic meter begins on a stress. Blake's Tyger Tyger burning bright opens each line with a heavy beat — urgent, incantatory.

Hiawatha (Longfellow) sustains trochaic tetrameter for hundreds of lines.
